N-mixture abundance with tulpaObs

Source: vignettes/abundance.Rmd
abundance.Rmd
library(tulpaObs)

From presence to counts

Occupancy models ask one question per site: is the species there or not. A repeated-count survey asks a harder one. A surveyor visits a site five times and records not whether a marbled salamander was seen, but how many: 3, then 1, then 4, then 0, then 2. Those numbers carry more than presence. They carry the size of the local population, blurred by the fact that nobody counts every individual on every visit.

Royle’s (2004) N-mixture model is the tool for that data. It keeps the two-level structure occupancy taught us, a true state we cannot see and a noisy observation we can, but the latent state is now a count rather than a coin flip. Each site holds some unknown number of animals NiN_i, fixed across the short survey window. On each visit the surveyor detects each animal independently with probability pijp_{ij}, so the recorded count yijy_{ij} is a thinned version of NiN_i. Five visits to a site with eight animals and detection 0.4 might read 4, 2, 3, 4, 1. The counts never reach eight, and the model’s job is to see eight through the thinning.

This buys you something occupancy cannot give. Where occupancy estimates the probability a site is used, N-mixture estimates how many individuals use it, and how that number responds to a covariate, all from counts that systematically undercount. The price is the same identifiability tension occupancy has, sharpened: abundance and detection both push the counts down or up, and the data have to separate them. A site that averages two animals per visit is consistent with twenty animals seen one in ten times, or with three animals seen two in three times. What breaks the tie is the spread of the counts across visits. Twenty animals at detection 0.1 produce counts that jump around a lot relative to their mean; three animals at detection 0.67 produce counts that barely move. The model reads that spread and infers the abundance behind it. More visits sharpen the read, and counts that vary across them are what carry the information at all.

The model leans on one assumption worth naming up front: the population is closed across the survey window. The NiN_i animals at a site stay put and stay the same animals from the first visit to the last, so every count is a thinning of the same latent number. A survey spread over a season that lets animals move in and out, breed, or die violates this, and the model will read the movement as detection noise. The closure window is usually a few days to a few weeks, short enough that the standing population is fixed but long enough to gather replicate counts. Designing the survey to respect that window matters as much as any modelling choice that follows.

This vignette builds an N-mixture fit from a simulation with known truth, reads the estimates back, handles the count-ceiling parameter, switches to a negative-binomial state for overdispersed counts, predicts abundance at new covariate values, adds an areal spatial field, and closes with the rules of thumb that decide when the model is the right one.

The model

Write the two levels for site ii and visit jj. The latent abundance is Poisson with a log-linear mean, and the counts are binomial thinnings of that abundance with a logit-linear detection:

Ni∼Poisson(λi),log⁡λi=xi⊤βλ,yij∣Ni∼Binomial(Ni,pij),logitpij=wij⊤βp. \begin{aligned} N_i &\sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_i), & \log \lambda_i &= x_i^\top \beta_\lambda, \\ y_{ij} \mid N_i &\sim \mathrm{Binomial}(N_i, p_{ij}), & \mathrm{logit}\, p_{ij} &= w_{ij}^\top \beta_p. \end{aligned}

Here λi\lambda_i is the expected abundance at site ii, driven by site covariates xix_i through a log link, and pijp_{ij} is the per-individual detection probability on visit jj, driven by detection covariates wijw_{ij} through a logit link. The abundance arm uses a log link because λ\lambda is a rate that must stay positive; that detail comes back the first time you read a coefficient.

The latent NiN_i never appears in the data. What occupancy did with a single sum over {0,1}\{0, 1\}, N-mixture does with a sum over every possible abundance:

p(yi⋅∣λi,pi⋅)=∑N=maxjyijKPoisson(N∣λi)∏jBinomial(yij∣N,pij). p(y_{i\cdot} \mid \lambda_i, p_{i\cdot}) \;=\; \sum_{N = \max_j y_{ij}}^{K} \mathrm{Poisson}(N \mid \lambda_i) \prod_j \mathrm{Binomial}(y_{ij} \mid N, p_{ij}).

The sum runs from the largest count seen at the site (you cannot have fewer animals than you counted on your best visit) up to a ceiling KK. This marginal has a closed form, so tulpa evaluates it directly with analytical gradients and reads the curvature at the mode for standard errors. There is no EM loop and no data augmentation over NN: the latent count integrates out exactly, term by term, which is why the fit returns in a fraction of a second. The ceiling KK is the one approximation, and the next sections treat it as such.

The exact marginalisation is what separates this from occupancy mechanically. An occupancy model sums over two states and the arithmetic is trivial. An N-mixture model sums over a few hundred, and a naive implementation would recompute the binomial product for every candidate NN at every site on every gradient step. tulpa caches the parts of each term that do not depend on the coefficients, so the repeated evaluations across the optimisation reuse work rather than redo it. The practical effect is that a fit on a few hundred sites with a ceiling in the low hundreds is a sub-second operation, not a sampler you wait on. The same closed form also means the standard errors are the genuine observed-information curvature of the marginal, not a Monte-Carlo approximation, so the credible intervals are deterministic and repeatable across runs.

One consequence of the log link deserves a flag before the first fit. A coefficient on the abundance arm is a multiplicative effect on expected abundance, not an additive one. A slope of 0.5 means a one-unit increase in the covariate multiplies λ\lambda by e0.5≈1.65e^{0.5} \approx 1.65, a 65 percent rise, and the same slope adds more animals where abundance is already high than where it is low. The intercept is the log of baseline abundance, so it reads as a number of animals only after exp(). This is the same arithmetic a Poisson GLM uses, and the coefficients carry the same interpretation; the only twist is that the counts feeding them are thinned, and the model corrects for the thinning before it reports the slope.

Simulating and fitting a Poisson model

simulate_abun() draws a dataset with the truth you set, so the fit has a target to recover. Abundance depends on one site covariate with intercept log⁡3\log 3 (so baseline expected abundance is 3 animals) and slope 0.5; detection depends on one covariate with intercept 0.4 (detection near 0.6) and slope 0.3. Five visits per site give the thinning enough replication to separate the two arms.

sa <- simulate_abun(
  N = 200, J = 5,
  n_abund_covs = 1, n_det_covs = 1,
  beta_lambda = c(log(3), 0.5),   # log link: intercept is log(baseline lambda)
  beta_p      = c(0.4, 0.3),      # logit link on detection
  seed = 2
)
dat <- sa$data       # site covariates, one row per site
y   <- sa$y          # 200 x 5 count matrix
y[1:4, ]

The counts undercount the latent abundance. Averaging the per-site maximum count against the simulated truth shows the gap that detection opens.

c(mean_max_count = mean(apply(y, 1, max)),
  mean_true_N    = mean(sa$truth$N))

The fit follows the same call shape as occupancy. The abundance formula is the first argument, detection is its own formula, and abun() selects the N-mixture family. method = "laplace" is the default; it finds the mode of the marginal likelihood and the curvature there. A shared areal field fits under method = "nested_laplace" (used in the spatial section below), and method = "nuts" samples the closed-form marginal in full when you want the whole posterior rather than the Laplace approximation.

fa <- tobs(
  ~ abund_cov1,
  data      = dat,
  family    = abun(),
  detection = ~ det_cov1,
  y         = y,
  method    = "laplace",
  control   = list(verbose = FALSE)   # the fitter prints iterations otherwise
)

coef() returns the estimates named by arm (lambda_, p_). Read the lambda arm with the log link in mind: the intercept is on the log scale, so back-transforming with exp() gives baseline expected abundance.

coef(fa)
c(baseline_lambda = exp(coef(fa, arm = "lambda")[["(Intercept)"]]),
  true_baseline   = 3)

The abundance intercept back-transforms to roughly the three animals the data were built with, and the slope on abund_cov1 lands near the simulated 0.5. summary() adds the posterior standard deviation and the credible bounds for every coefficient; the lambda_ rows are the abundance arm and the p_ rows the detection arm.

summary(fa)

fitted() returns the per-site quantities the fit implies: expected abundance lambda, detection probability p, and the posterior mean abundance N given the counts. The last one is the estimate that matters for a population total, since it conditions on what was actually seen at each site.

fv <- fitted(fa)
str(lapply(fv, head, 4))

Plotting the posterior mean abundance against the simulated truth shows the model recovers the site-level signal through the thinning, not just the population average.

plot(sa$truth$N, fv$N, pch = 16, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.35),
     xlab = "true N", ylab = "fitted E[N | y]")
abline(0, 1, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)

The points track the identity line with scatter that grows at higher abundance, which is the right behaviour: a site with more animals leaves more room for the binomial thinning to vary the counts, so its posterior abundance is less certain.

The count ceiling K_max

The marginal likelihood sums over abundance from each site’s maximum count up to a ceiling. That ceiling is K_max, and the fit chooses a default from the data when you do not set it. The sum has to reach high enough that the Poisson mass above K_max is negligible; if K_max sits too close to the true abundance, the model truncates probability that belongs in the likelihood and biases λ\lambda downward.

The default works for ordinary counts. You raise K_max when abundance is large relative to detection, so the latent NN can sit far above any single count. A site with λ=40\lambda = 40 and detection 0.2 might never record more than a dozen animals on a visit, yet its abundance routinely exceeds thirty, and the sum has to climb past that. The symptom of a ceiling set too low is a boundary warning or an abundance estimate that drifts when you raise it. The check is to refit with a higher K_max and confirm the estimate is stable.

fa_k <- tobs(~ abund_cov1, data = dat, family = abun(),
             detection = ~ det_cov1, y = y, method = "laplace",
             control = list(verbose = FALSE), K_max = 200)
rbind(default_K = coef(fa, arm = "lambda"),
      K_max_200 = coef(fa_k, arm = "lambda"))

The two fits agree to several decimals, so the default ceiling was already high enough here. On data where they disagree, take the higher-K_max fit and keep raising it until the estimate settles. The cost of a generous ceiling is compute time, since the inner sum runs over more terms, and that cost is linear in K_max, so a ceiling a few times the largest plausible abundance is a safe default rather than an expensive one.

It helps to see why a low ceiling pulls the estimate down. The likelihood asks how probable the observed counts are under a given λ\lambda, and it answers by summing over every abundance that could have produced them. If the true λ\lambda wants to place real probability on abundances above the ceiling, cutting the sum off there throws that probability away. The optimiser then finds a smaller λ\lambda that fits its mass entirely below the ceiling, and the abundance estimate comes out biased low. The bias is invisible in any single fit; it shows only when you raise the ceiling and watch the estimate move. That is why the stability check is the diagnostic rather than any one number. A practical starting point is to set K_max to several times the largest count you would believe at the most abundant site, then confirm a doubling of it leaves the coefficients unchanged. The negative-binomial state, with its heavier tail, needs more headroom than Poisson for the same mean, so a ceiling that suffices under Poisson can be tight under overdispersion.

Overdispersion and the negative binomial

The Poisson state assumes the variance of abundance equals its mean. Real populations rarely oblige. Animals cluster, habitat varies in ways no covariate captures, and the spread of true abundance across sites runs wider than Poisson allows. When it does, a Poisson N-mixture absorbs the extra spread into λ\lambda and detection, and the standard errors come out too small.

The biology behind overdispersion is worth holding in mind, because it tells you when to expect it. A Poisson abundance is what you get when individuals settle independently and at the same rate everywhere a covariate says they should. Real animals do neither. They aggregate around resources, they respond to gradients no survey measured, and a good patch holds far more than its covariates predict while a poor one holds far fewer. Each of those produces sites that are more variable than their fitted mean, which is overdispersion exactly. The clustering need not be spatial; it can be any unmeasured driver that makes some sites richer and others poorer than the covariates explain. Whenever you suspect such a driver, and in count data you usually should, the negative binomial is the safer default state.

abun(mixture = "negbin") replaces the Poisson state with a negative binomial, Ni∼NegBin(λi,r)N_i \sim \mathrm{NegBin}(\lambda_i, r), where the size rr sets the overdispersion through Var(N)=λ+λ2/r\mathrm{Var}(N) = \lambda + \lambda^2 / r. A small rr means heavy clustering; as rr grows the negative binomial approaches the Poisson, and the extra parameter costs nothing. Simulate overdispersed counts with r=2r = 2, so a site with mean abundance 4 has variance 4+16/2=124 + 16/2 = 12, three times the Poisson value.

sb <- simulate_abun(
  N = 200, J = 5, n_abund_covs = 1, n_det_covs = 1,
  mixture = "negbin", size = 2,
  beta_lambda = c(log(4), 0.4), beta_p = c(0.5, 0.2),
  seed = 5
)

Fit the negative-binomial model by passing the same mixture flag to the family. The size rr is estimated jointly with the coefficients on the log scale and reported on the object.

fb <- tobs(~ abund_cov1, data = sb$data, family = abun(mixture = "negbin"),
           detection = ~ det_cov1, y = sb$y, method = "laplace",
           control = list(verbose = FALSE))
coef(fb)

The dispersion lives in fb$nmix_dispersion: the natural-scale size $r, its log-scale value $log_r, and the delta-method standard error $r_sd.

fb$nmix_dispersion

The estimated rr sits near the simulated 2, with a standard error wide enough to tell you the size is the least certain quantity in the fit. That is normal. The size is identified only through the tail of the count distribution, and a single dataset of 200 sites pins it loosely.

Fitting a negative binomial when the data are actually Poisson is close to free, since the size simply drifts large. Fitting a Poisson when the data are overdispersed is the costly mistake, because the missing variance has nowhere to go but the standard errors. A quick dispersion check tells you which regime you are in. Compare the variance of the per-site maximum count against its mean: a ratio well above one is the signature of overdispersion that a Poisson state cannot represent.

maxcount <- apply(sb$y, 1, max)
c(mean = mean(maxcount), var = var(maxcount),
  ratio = var(maxcount) / mean(maxcount))

A ratio near one says Poisson will do; a ratio of two or more says reach for the negative binomial. This is a rough diagnostic on the observed counts, not the latent state, so treat it as a flag rather than a test. The cleaner comparison is to fit both and read the marginal log-likelihood, which the next-to-last section does.

Predicting abundance

predict() with a design matrix X.0 returns the abundance arm’s prediction at new covariate values, on the response scale, with the posterior spread propagated through the joint coefficient covariance. Pass one column per abundance coefficient.

X0 <- cbind(`(Intercept)` = 1, abund_cov1 = c(-1.5, 0, 1.5))
predict(fa, X.0 = X0)

Expected abundance climbs across the three covariate values, and the credible bounds widen with the mean, the multiplicative spread a log link produces. That widening is what the log link means. A fixed uncertainty on the log scale becomes a proportional uncertainty on the count scale, so a prediction of 8 animals carries a wider absolute band than a prediction of 2, even when the coefficient is equally well known. Reading the bounds on the response scale, as predict() returns them, keeps that proportionality visible rather than hiding it on the log scale where it looks constant.

The draws behind these summaries come from the joint coefficient covariance, so the abundance and detection arms vary together rather than independently. This matters for any quantity that combines the two, a detection-corrected total or a ratio of abundances at two covariate values, because the two arms are negatively correlated through the counts: a fit that nudges detection up has to nudge abundance down to match the same counts. Drawing them jointly propagates that correlation into the derived quantity, where drawing them separately would overstate its uncertainty. To trace the response across the whole covariate range rather than at three points, pass terms and the predictor name; the result carries an estimate and a band at each grid point, ready to plot.

pr <- predict(fa, terms = "abund_cov1")
plot(pr$x, pr$estimate, type = "n",
     xlab = "abund_cov1", ylab = "expected abundance",
     ylim = range(pr$lower, pr$upper))
polygon(c(pr$x, rev(pr$x)), c(pr$lower, rev(pr$upper)),
        col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.25), border = NA)
lines(pr$x, pr$estimate, lwd = 2)

The band is the abundance arm’s uncertainty alone. The detection arm has its own prediction surface, reached with type = "detection", which is the right call when the question is about survey efficiency rather than population size.

predict(fa, X.0 = cbind(`(Intercept)` = 1, det_cov1 = c(-1, 0, 1)),
        type = "detection")

Random effects on abundance

Counts arrive grouped. Sites cluster into watersheds, plots nest inside forest stands, transects fall under the field crew that walked them. The group carries its own baseline abundance that no measured covariate captures, and treating that grouping as one fixed intercept per level burns a parameter on every group and leaves the sparse ones with wild estimates. A random intercept ties the levels together instead: each group’s abundance baseline is a draw from N(0,σ2)N(0, \sigma^2), and the model estimates the single spread σ\sigma rather than one free intercept per group. Groups with many sites keep their own signal; groups with few are pulled toward the population mean, the shrinkage that is the point of the random effect rather than a side effect of it.

abun() carries the lme4 bar syntax on either arm. A term in the abundance formula varies log-abundance by group; a term in the detection formula varies the logit of detection. The single-species N-mixture takes (1 | g) for a random intercept and the slope variants (x | g), (x || g), and (1 + x | g) the same way the occupancy model does, with one restriction: a term cannot sit on both arms of one fit, and a random effect cannot share a fit with an areal spatial field. Either of those needs the joint sampler. Put the bar on one arm at a time and the deterministic path handles it.

Simulate grouped abundance with eight watersheds, each holding its own log-abundance offset drawn from N(0,0.62)N(0, 0.6^2), on top of a site covariate x1. Detection is constant near 0.5, and four visits give the thinning enough replication.

sim_re <- function(N = 120, J = 4, ngrp = 8, sigma_b = 0.6, seed = 11) {
  set.seed(seed)
  grp <- rep(seq_len(ngrp), length.out = N)
  b   <- rnorm(ngrp, sd = sigma_b)
  dat <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(N), g = factor(grp))
  eta <- as.numeric(model.matrix(~ x1, dat) %*% c(0.6, 0.4)) + b[grp]
  Nlat <- rpois(N, exp(eta))
  y <- matrix(NA_integer_, N, J)
  for (i in seq_len(N)) y[i, ] <- rbinom(J, Nlat[i], plogis(0))
  list(y = y, data = dat, b = b)
}
sr <- sim_re()

The fit reads like the others, with the bar inside the abundance formula. control = list(n.quad = 5) sets the adaptive Gauss-Hermite resolution that debiases the small-cluster variance attenuation; n.quad = 1 is the plain joint Laplace, and higher values recover the spread the single Gaussian per group misses.

fr <- tobs(
  ~ x1 + (1 | g),
  data      = sr$data,
  family    = abun(),
  detection = ~ 1,
  y         = sr$y,
  method    = "laplace",
  control   = list(n.quad = 5, verbose = FALSE)
)
coef(fr, arm = "lambda")

The abundance intercept and slope recover near the simulated 0.6 and 0.4 with the group structure absorbed into the random effect rather than blended into the coefficients. The variance component lives in fr$means under a sigma_g-prefixed name, the spread across watershed baselines.

sig_name <- grep("^sigma_g", names(fr$means), value = TRUE)
c(estimate = fr$means[[sig_name]], truth = 0.6)

vcov() returns the joint fixed-effect covariance over the abundance and detection coefficients alone, the same block the non-grouped fit carries. The variance-component point estimate sits outside it, since the marginal-Hessian path does not surface its joint posterior covariance with the fixed effects.

round(vcov(fr), 4)

ranef() returns the per-group effects, the BLUPs, one row per group level and coefficient: the grouping factor, the level, the term, the estimate, and its standard error. The standard error is the genuine AGHQ marginal posterior spread, wider for groups with fewer sites.

re <- ranef(fr)
re

Plot the recovered group effects against the simulated truth with the BLUP standard error as an interval. The points track the identity line, with the shrinkage that pulls sparse groups toward zero and the uncertainty band that widens where a group carries less data.

library(ggplot2)
re$truth <- sr$b[as.integer(re$level)]
ggplot(re, aes(truth, estimate)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - std.error, ymax = estimate + std.error),
                width = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "true group effect", y = "estimated BLUP") +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent"),
        plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "transparent"))

The same machinery moves to detection by writing the bar in the detection formula, where it varies the per-group logit of detection and the variance component is named sigma_p for the detection arm. Under mixture = "negbin" the random effect and the overdispersion size are estimated together on the same AGHQ likelihood, with the size as the trailing log-scale coordinate. The recovery here used eight groups; the variance starts to mean something around five to eight levels, and below that a fixed effect that names each group is the honest choice.

Counts on a map

Sites near each other often hold similar numbers of animals for reasons no covariate records: shared microclimate, a corridor of good habitat, a patch the survey design happened to cluster. Left unmodelled, that structure does two kinds of damage. It inflates confidence in the slopes, because neighbouring sites carry correlated leftovers and the model counts each as fresh information when they are partly the same observation seen twice. And it biases the slopes themselves whenever a covariate is spatially patterned, since the covariate and the unmeasured regional driver vary together and a model with nowhere to put the driver loads it onto the covariate. An areal spatial field gives the regional signal a place to live, one random effect per spatial unit, tied to neighbours so the surface stays smooth. The slope is then read against a background that already accounts for location, and its standard error widens to its honest size because the field, not the covariate, now carries the autocorrelation.

The same logic that motivates a spatial field for a binomial or Gaussian response carries over to counts unchanged. What differs is only where the field attaches: it enters the log-abundance predictor, alongside the covariate slopes, so it soaks up the regional variation in how many animals a site holds. The detection arm is left non-spatial here, which is the usual choice, since detection is a property of the survey rather than the place. If survey effort is itself spatially clustered, a field on detection is possible too, but the common case puts the field on abundance and reads it as the smoothed map of population density the covariates do not explain.

For N-mixture the field attaches to the abundance arm through a spatial term inside the formula, with method = "nested_laplace". The areal terms are icar(), bym2(), and car_proper(); each takes a dense 0/1 adjacency matrix with one row and column per site. Build a small grid and its rook adjacency, where each cell neighbours the cells directly above, below, left, and right.

grid_adj <- function(side) {
  ng <- side * side
  co <- expand.grid(x = seq_len(side), y = seq_len(side))
  adj <- matrix(0L, ng, ng)
  for (i in seq_len(ng)) for (j in seq_len(ng)) {
    if (i != j && abs(co$x[i] - co$x[j]) + abs(co$y[i] - co$y[j]) == 1L)
      adj[i, j] <- 1L
  }
  adj
}
adj <- grid_adj(6)        # 36 cells, one site per cell
dim(adj)

Simulate counts on the grid with a smooth abundance field added to the log-linear mean, then thin them to visits. The field is the regional signal the fit has to recover alongside the covariate slope.

sim_spatial <- function(adj, b_lambda, b_p, J = 5, sd_phi = 0.6, seed = NULL) {
  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)
  ng <- nrow(adj)
  phi <- as.numeric(scale(rnorm(ng)))
  for (rep in 1:3) {                       # smooth toward neighbours
    pn <- phi
    for (i in seq_len(ng)) {
      nb <- which(adj[i, ] == 1L)
      pn[i] <- 0.5 * phi[i] + 0.5 * mean(phi[nb])
    }
    phi <- pn
  }
  phi <- sd_phi * as.numeric(scale(phi)); phi <- phi - mean(phi)
  x_ab <- rnorm(ng); x_det <- rnorm(ng)
  lambda <- exp(b_lambda[1] + b_lambda[2] * x_ab + phi)
  p <- plogis(b_p[1] + b_p[2] * x_det)
  N <- rpois(ng, lambda)
  y <- matrix(NA_integer_, ng, J)
  for (i in seq_len(ng)) y[i, ] <- rbinom(J, N[i], p[i])
  list(y = y, data = data.frame(abund_cov1 = x_ab, det_cov1 = x_det),
       phi = phi)
}
ss <- sim_spatial(adj, b_lambda = c(log(5), 0.5), b_p = c(0.3, 0.4), seed = 42)

Fit the spatial model with a bym2() term on the abundance formula. The field’s smoothing strength is integrated over a grid rather than fixed, so the slope standard errors carry the field’s own uncertainty. The fit returns the same tobs_fit object as the non-spatial path, with fs$method reading "nested_laplace".

fs <- suppressWarnings(tobs(
  ~ abund_cov1 + bym2(graph = adj),
  data      = ss$data,
  family    = abun(),
  detection = ~ det_cov1,
  y         = ss$y,
  method    = "nested_laplace",
  control   = list(verbose = FALSE, max.iter = 50)
))
coef(fs)

The covariate slopes recover with the regional signal absorbed into the field rather than blended into the coefficient: coef(fs) reads back the abundance slope near the simulated 0.5 and the detection slope near 0.4.

Read the slopes, not the abundance intercept, under an intrinsic field. The intrinsic prior pins the field only up to an overall level, so the intercept and the field mean trade off along a flat direction; the BYM2 field’s independent component tames that confounding but the slopes are the inferential payload regardless. The recovered field comes back on the object as fs$spatial_field, one value per cell, and cor(fs$spatial_field, ss$phi) is positive: the fit cannot reconstruct one draw of a noisy field exactly, but it recovers its shape, and that shape is what removes the bias from the slopes.

c(field_cor = cor(fs$spatial_field, ss$phi),
  method    = fs$method)

Under mixture = "negbin" the size rr is integrated over the outer grid alongside the field’s smoothing parameters and reported in fs$nmix_hyper$r rather than as a coefficient, so the spatial path handles overdispersion without adding a fixed parameter to the covariance.

Comparing models and practical guidance

Does the negative binomial earn its extra parameter? Fit both states on the overdispersed data and read the marginal log-likelihood through logLik(). The marginal already integrates the latent abundance out, so a higher value means the state genuinely fits the counts better, not that it has more freedom.

fb_pois <- tobs(~ abund_cov1, data = sb$data, family = abun(),
                detection = ~ det_cov1, y = sb$y, method = "laplace",
                control = list(verbose = FALSE))

c(poisson = as.numeric(logLik(fb_pois)),
  negbin  = as.numeric(logLik(fb)))

The negative binomial carries the higher log-likelihood on data built with r=2r = 2, which is the answer the simulation should give. On real data the same comparison decides the state: a meaningfully higher negative-binomial log-likelihood says the counts are overdispersed and the Poisson was hiding it in the standard errors. A near-tie says Poisson is adequate and the simpler state is the honest choice.

A handful of rules of thumb make the rest of the modelling decisions.

  • At least three visits, more when detection is low. The abundance and detection arms separate only through the spread of counts across visits. With two visits and detection below about 0.3 they are weakly identified, and the abundance estimate can drift toward the count ceiling or collapse toward the mean count. Three visits is the practical floor; five or more is comfortable, and they buy more than extra sites do because replication, not site count, is what pins detection.

  • Counts must vary within a site. A site that reads 2, 2, 2, 2 tells the model almost nothing about detection, since constant counts are consistent with high abundance and high detection or low abundance seen perfectly. Variation across visits is the signal the binomial thinning leaves, and it is what the detection arm reads. If your counts barely move across visits, the fit will lean on the prior and the covariates rather than the data.

  • Check the dispersion before trusting Poisson standard errors. A variance-to-mean ratio of the per-site counts above roughly two is a flag for the negative binomial. Fitting Poisson on overdispersed counts does not bias the slopes badly, but it understates their uncertainty, so a coefficient can read significant when it is not. When in doubt, fit both and compare the marginal log-likelihood.

  • Raise K_max when abundance dwarfs detection. The default ceiling suits ordinary counts. When expected abundance is large and detection is small, the latent NN sits far above any visit’s count, and a ceiling set too low truncates the likelihood and biases λ\lambda down. A workable rule is to set K_max to roughly three to five times the largest count you would believe at the richest site, then double it and confirm the coefficients do not move. The negative-binomial state needs the upper end of that range for the same mean, since its heavier tail puts mass higher.

  • Group with five to eight levels before trusting the variance. A random effect on the abundance arm estimates the spread across groups, and with two or three groups there is almost no information about that spread. Five to eight levels is the rough floor; below it, name each group with a fixed intercept instead. Keep at least ten sites per group when the term carries a random slope rather than only an intercept, since a slope asks each group’s own data to inform its covariate effect before shrinkage.

  • When N-mixture is the wrong tool. Three cases call for a different model. If the surveys are not closed, animals moving in and out between visits so abundance is not fixed, the binomial thinning assumption breaks and the model reads movement as detection. If you only have detection or non-detection rather than counts, occupancy is the honest model and N-mixture adds a latent abundance the data cannot inform. And if detection is near one, the counts are nearly the abundance itself, so a plain Poisson or negative-binomial regression on the counts is simpler and loses nothing.
